title: What Is Life?
text: Biologists use a set of shared characteristics to decide whether something is alive. Living things are made of one or more cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their environment, reproduce, and maintain a stable internal environment, a process called homeostasis. Populations of living things also change over many generations through evolution. A virus shows some of these characteristics but cannot reproduce on its own, so many scientists do not classify viruses as living.

title: The Scientific Method
text: Science begins with an observation that leads to a question. A hypothesis is a testable explanation for the observation. Scientists design a controlled experiment that changes one variable, the independent variable, and measures its effect on another, the dependent variable. All other conditions are held constant. A control group receives no treatment so results can be compared. When many experiments support a hypothesis, it may become part of a broader theory.

title: Water and Life
text: Water is a polar molecule: the oxygen side has a slight negative charge and the hydrogen side has a slight positive charge. This lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. Hydrogen bonds give water a high specific heat, so it changes temperature slowly and helps organisms stay stable. Water is also an excellent solvent, which means many substances dissolve in it, so it can carry nutrients and wastes inside living things.

title: Macromolecules
text: Four kinds of large molecules, called macromolecules, are found in all living things. Carbohydrates, such as glucose and starch, provide quick energy. Lipids, such as fats and phospholipids, store energy and form cell membranes. Proteins are chains of amino acids; their shapes let them act as enzymes, structures, and signals. Nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, store and use genetic information. Each macromolecule is built from smaller units called monomers.

title: Cell Structure
text: All cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, have no nucleus. Eukaryotic cells, such as plant and animal cells, keep their DNA inside a nucleus and contain organelles with specific jobs. Mitochondria release energy from food. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus make and ship proteins. Plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

title: History of the Microscope
text: Optional reading. In the 1600s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used handmade lenses to observe tiny living organisms in pond water. Robert Hooke looked at thin slices of cork and named the small boxes he saw cells. Later improvements in lenses and staining made it possible to see structures inside cells. Today, electron microscopes can show details far smaller than light microscopes can.

title: How Things Cross the Membrane
text: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, which means it lets some substances pass and blocks others. In diffusion, molecules move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration without using energy. Osmosis is the diffusion of water. Facilitated diffusion uses transport proteins but still needs no energy. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy in the form of ATP.

title: Enzymes
text: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy needed to start them. Each enzyme has an active site that fits a specific substrate. Temperature and pH affect enzyme shape; if conditions are too extreme, the enzyme can denature and stop working. Enzymes are not used up in reactions, so one enzyme can be used many times.

title: Photosynthesis
text: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts. Plants use light energy, water, and carbon dioxide to make glucose and release oxygen. In the light-dependent reactions, light energy splits water and makes ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, the plant uses ATP and NADPH to turn carbon dioxide into sugar. Photosynthesis is the main way energy enters most food chains.

title: Plants in Space
text: Optional reading. Astronauts have grown lettuce and other plants on the International Space Station. Without gravity, roots and shoots use light to decide which way to grow. Researchers study these plants to learn how to grow food on long missions.
